name: Terravox
tagline: Your codebase, speaking back to you
description: Terravox turns codebases into conversational interfaces. Engineers ask questions in plain English and get answers grounded in their actual code — not generic docs. Built for teams drowning in tribal knowledge.
mission:
Every engineering team has a dark matter problem. The most critical knowledge — why that service was split, which edge case broke prod last November, how the auth flow actually works — lives in Slack threads, PR comments, and the heads of three people who've been here since day one.

Terravox exists because we believe code should be its own documentation. Not through comments or wikis that rot the moment they're written, but through a living intelligence layer that reads your entire codebase, your git history, your design docs, and your incident reports — and answers questions as if it were your most senior engineer.

We're not building another code search tool. We're building institutional memory for engineering organizations. When a new hire asks "how does billing work?", they should get the same quality answer at 2am on a Saturday that they'd get sitting next to your staff engineer on a Tuesday.

Our founding team spent a combined 30 years at infrastructure companies watching brilliant engineers waste hours reverse-engineering systems that someone else already understood. We're fixing that by making codebases conversational — not as a novelty, but as the primary interface for understanding complex software systems.

The future we're building toward is one where onboarding takes days instead of months, where incident response is guided by full system context, and where the bus factor of any team approaches infinity.
marketResearch:
The developer productivity market has ballooned to $22B globally, with AI-assisted development tools growing at 34% CAGR. The specific niche of codebase intelligence — tools that provide deep understanding of existing codebases rather than generating new code — is nascent but rapidly emerging, with an addressable market of roughly $6B across enterprise engineering teams.

Our SAM focuses on engineering organizations with 30+ developers running microservice architectures where knowledge fragmentation is acute. This represents approximately $2.1B in annual spend. Our initial SOM targets Series B-D startups and mid-market tech companies in North America, representing $350M in near-term opportunity.

The competitive landscape is bifurcated: on one side, code search tools like Sourcegraph and GitHub Code Search offer syntactic search but no semantic understanding. On the other, AI coding assistants like GitHub Copilot and Cursor focus on code generation rather than comprehension. Terravox occupies the gap — deep codebase understanding delivered through natural language. Our moat is the proprietary knowledge graph that connects code, git history, CI/CD data, and documentation into a unified semantic model.

Early traction includes design partnerships with two Series C infrastructure companies and one public fintech, all reporting 60%+ reduction in time spent on code archaeology. Our PLG motion starts with a free tier for open-source projects, converting to team plans when private repos are connected. Enterprise contracts include SSO, audit logs, and self-hosted deployment.

name: Patchwork
tagline: Stitch your tools together without writing glue code
description: Patchwork is a visual workflow builder that connects internal tools, APIs, and databases into automated pipelines. Think Zapier, but for engineering teams who need conditional logic, error handling, and observability built in.
mission:
Engineering teams are drowning in glue code. For every core system they build, there are dozens of scripts, cron jobs, and webhook handlers that shuttle data between tools, trigger notifications, and keep the machine running. This connective tissue is unglamorous, undertested, and the first thing to break.

Patchwork was born from a simple observation: most of this glue code follows predictable patterns. Extract data from A, transform it, load it into B, handle errors, alert if something breaks. Yet every team rebuilds these patterns from scratch, scattered across Lambda functions and GitHub Actions that nobody wants to own.

We're building a visual workflow engine that treats integrations as first-class infrastructure. Our canvas lets engineers design complex, multi-step automations with branching logic, retry policies, and real-time observability — all without sacrificing the power that code provides. When you need custom logic, drop into TypeScript or Python within any node.

We're not trying to replace engineering. We're trying to free engineers from the maintenance burden of the 80% of automation that shouldn't require bespoke code. Our dream is that every internal process — from onboarding flows to data pipeline orchestration to incident response — lives in a Patchwork workflow that anyone on the team can understand, modify, and debug.
marketResearch:
The workflow automation and iPaaS market is valued at $13.4B in 2025, projected to hit $32B by 2030 at 19% CAGR. Consumer-oriented platforms (Zapier, Make) dominate SMB but lack the developer-grade features enterprises need. Enterprise iPaaS tools (MuleSoft, Boomi) are powerful but require months of implementation and cost six figures annually.

Patchwork targets the underserved middle: engineering teams at companies with 50-2,000 employees who need robust automation without enterprise iPaaS overhead. This segment represents a $4.8B SAM. Our initial SOM — Series A-C tech companies and mid-market SaaS businesses in North America — is approximately $600M.

Competitors include Zapier (40M+ users but lacks error handling, branching, and observability), n8n (open-source, strong community but limited enterprise features), Temporal (excellent for orchestration but requires deep engineering investment), and Retool Workflows (good UI but tightly coupled to Retool ecosystem). Patchwork differentiates by combining visual design with production-grade reliability — built-in retry policies, dead letter queues, execution traces, and version-controlled workflow definitions stored as code.

Our GTM strategy is bottom-up developer adoption. Engineers discover Patchwork when searching for workflow automation, start with the free tier (up to 1,000 executions/month), and upgrade when they need team collaboration, SSO, and higher throughput. We convert to annual contracts through platform engineering leads who see Patchwork reducing their team's operational burden.

name: Mintlayer
tagline: API docs that developers actually want to read
description: Mintlayer generates beautiful, interactive API documentation from your OpenAPI specs with built-in playground, SDK generation, and changelog tracking. No more stale Swagger pages.
mission:
Documentation is where developer experience goes to die. Companies invest millions in building elegant APIs, then ship them with auto-generated Swagger UIs that look like tax forms. The result: frustrated developers, endless support tickets, and integration timelines measured in weeks instead of hours.

Mintlayer exists because we believe API documentation should be a product, not an afterthought. We take your OpenAPI spec and transform it into a developer portal that's as polished as your landing page — with interactive request builders, real-time playground environments, auto-generated SDKs in seven languages, and changelogs that track every breaking change.

We're a team of developer advocates and API designers who spent years on the other side of bad documentation. We know that the difference between a 5-minute integration and a 5-day integration is almost never the API's complexity — it's how well the docs communicate the happy path, the edge cases, and the mental model behind the design.

Our long-term vision extends beyond documentation into the full API lifecycle. We want Mintlayer to be where developers discover, evaluate, and integrate with APIs — a developer portal that reduces time-to-first-API-call from hours to seconds.
marketResearch:
The API management market is projected to reach $41B by 2030, with developer portals and documentation tools representing roughly $3.2B of that. The shift toward API-first companies has created massive demand for better developer experience tooling. Our TAM includes every company with a public or partner API — estimated at $3.2B. Our SAM narrows to mid-market and enterprise API-first companies with 5+ public endpoints, representing $850M. Our SOM targets the US and European markets, roughly $200M.

Key competitors: Readme.com (market leader, strong brand but aging UI), Stoplight (design-first approach, weaker on hosted portals), Redocly (open-source core, limited collaboration features), and Swagger/SwaggerHub (ubiquitous but universally disliked UX). Mintlayer differentiates through three pillars: a design-forward portal that matches the quality of the best marketing sites, built-in SDK generation that stays in sync with spec changes, and a changelog system that auto-detects breaking changes and notifies affected consumers.

Our target buyer is the developer experience lead or VP Engineering at API-first companies. Sales motion is product-led: teams import their OpenAPI spec, see a beautiful portal in minutes, and upgrade for custom domains, team collaboration, and analytics. Enterprise deals add SSO, SLAs, and white-labeling.

name: Canopy
description: Canopy merges feature flagging with A/B testing in a single platform. Ship features behind flags, run experiments with statistical rigor, and make data-driven rollout decisions — all without stitching together LaunchDarkly and Amplitude.
mission:
The modern software release process is split-brained. Feature flags live in one tool. Experimentation lives in another. Analytics lives in a third. Engineers toggle flags in LaunchDarkly, set up experiments in Optimizely, and check results in Amplitude — switching between dashboards, duplicating targeting rules, and hoping the data lines up.

Canopy unifies this workflow. We believe that every feature rollout is an experiment, and every experiment needs a flag. By combining these capabilities in a single platform, we eliminate the coordination overhead that slows teams down and introduce statistical rigor into decisions that are currently made by gut feeling.

Our founders built experimentation infrastructure at Spotify and Netflix, where A/B testing is a cultural practice, not just a tool. We saw that even at these companies, the gap between "flag on" and "experiment complete" was filled with duct tape. At smaller companies, it's a chasm. Most teams ship features to 100% on day one and hope for the best.

We're building Canopy so that every team — not just those with dedicated experimentation platforms — can ship features safely, measure their impact, and make rollout decisions with confidence. Progressive rollouts should be the default, not a luxury.
marketResearch:
The feature management market is valued at $1.8B in 2025, growing at 25% CAGR to reach $5.5B by 2030. The experimentation/A/B testing market adds another $1.2B. The convergence of these categories — what we call "experimentation-aware feature management" — represents a $3B combined TAM. Our SAM targets product-led SaaS companies with 20+ engineers, approximately $900M. Initial SOM focusing on US-based Series A-C startups is $150M.

Primary competitors: LaunchDarkly ($3.4B valuation, market leader in flags but limited experimentation), Split.io (closest to our vision but complex setup and enterprise-only pricing), Statsig (strong experimentation but weaker flag management), and Eppo (analytics-first, less focus on flag operations). Open-source options like Unleash and Flagsmith cover basic flags but lack experimentation entirely.

Canopy's differentiation: unified flag+experiment lifecycle (create flag, define hypothesis, set rollout percentage, auto-analyze results, graduate or kill), Bayesian statistics engine that reaches significance faster than frequentist competitors, and a pricing model based on monthly tracked users rather than per-seat licensing.

GTM strategy: developer-led growth through excellent DX. Our SDK is a single line of code. Free tier supports up to 10,000 MTUs. We convert through product teams who want experiment results alongside their flag configuration. Enterprise motion targets VP Product and VP Engineering with compliance features and premium SLAs.

name: Overture
tagline: The operating system for product launches
description: Overture coordinates the chaos of product launches — syncing engineering, marketing, sales, and support across timelines, checklists, and go/no-go gates. One dashboard to replace the spreadsheet that nobody trusts.
mission:
Product launches are the highest-stakes cross-functional moment in any company. They involve engineering shipping code, marketing preparing campaigns, sales enabling reps, support writing help docs, legal reviewing terms, and leadership making go/no-go decisions. And all of this is coordinated in... a Google Sheet.

Overture exists because we've lived through the pain of launches managed by spreadsheets and Slack threads. We've seen launches slip because marketing didn't know engineering was a week behind. We've seen support tickets spike because help docs weren't updated. We've seen revenue targets missed because sales enablement started too late.

We're building a purpose-built coordination layer for product launches. Overture provides a shared timeline that every team can see, checklists that auto-assign tasks based on launch type, dependency tracking that surfaces blockers before they become emergencies, and go/no-go dashboards that give leadership a single source of truth.

Our vision goes beyond launches into the broader category of cross-functional coordination. Every company has high-stakes moments that require multiple teams to execute in sync — launches, migrations, compliance deadlines, annual planning. These moments deserve better tooling than spreadsheets and prayer.
marketResearch:
The project management software market is $7.2B and growing at 13% CAGR, but the specific niche of launch management and cross-functional coordination is underserved by existing tools. Jira, Asana, and Monday.com handle individual team workflows well but struggle with the cross-team coordination that launches require. The TAM for launch/program management tools is approximately $2B. Our SAM — product-led companies with 100-5,000 employees doing 4+ launches per year — is $650M. Our initial SOM targeting Series B+ SaaS companies is $120M.

Competitors include generic PM tools (Asana, Monday.com — too flexible, require heavy customization for launches), LaunchNotes (focused on changelog/release notes, not coordination), and Productboard (roadmap-focused, no execution layer). Overture differentiates as the only purpose-built launch coordination platform with cross-functional templates, automated dependency tracking, and integrated go/no-go workflows.

Target buyers are Heads of Product, PMOs, and Chiefs of Staff who own launch coordination today. Our sales motion starts with a free tier for individual launches, expanding to team plans for recurring launch programs. Enterprise deals include custom templates, integrations with Jira/Asana/Slack, and launch analytics.

name: Steno
tagline: Meeting intelligence that writes itself into your workflow
description: Steno records, transcribes, and extracts structured data from meetings — then pushes action items to Jira, decisions to Notion, and summaries to Slack. It's not another transcript. It's meeting-to-workflow automation.
mission:
The modern knowledge worker attends 15-20 meetings per week. Each meeting generates decisions, action items, and context that need to flow into project management tools, documentation, and communication channels. Today, that flow depends on someone taking notes and manually updating five different tools afterward. It rarely happens.

Steno was built on a radical premise: meetings shouldn't create work — they should complete it. When your team decides to push the launch date by a week, that decision should automatically update the Jira epic, notify the Slack channel, and create a Notion entry. When your manager assigns you a follow-up, it should appear in your task list without anyone copying and pasting.

We're not building a better transcription tool. We're building the connective tissue between what happens in meetings and what happens after them. Steno uses AI to extract structured data — decisions, action items, blockers, owners, deadlines — and routes them to the right tools with the right context.

Our team comes from backgrounds in NLP research and workflow automation. We believe meetings are the most underutilized data source in any organization. They contain the real decisions, the nuanced context, and the unwritten agreements that never make it into documentation. Steno's job is to capture that signal and make it actionable.
marketResearch:
The meeting technology market (recording, transcription, intelligence) is valued at $5.8B in 2025, projected to reach $12.1B by 2030 at 16% CAGR. Within this, the meeting intelligence sub-segment — tools that go beyond transcription to extract insights and automate follow-ups — is growing at 28% CAGR and represents a $2.4B opportunity.

Our SAM targets knowledge-work organizations with 50-5,000 employees where meetings are a primary coordination mechanism. This represents approximately $1.1B. Our initial SOM focuses on product and engineering teams at Series B+ tech companies, roughly $180M.

Competitor landscape: Otter.ai (largest player, strong transcription but limited action extraction), Fireflies.ai (good integrations but AI extraction is surface-level), Grain (video clips, good for sales but not for engineering/product), Fathom (free note-taking, no workflow automation). Steno differentiates through deep workflow integration — we don't just identify action items, we create Jira tickets with the right project, assignee, and context. Our extraction model is trained on meeting-specific language patterns ("let's circle back on this" = action item, "we decided to go with option B" = decision).

GTM is PLG. Steno works with Zoom, Google Meet, and Teams. Free tier records and transcribes up to 10 meetings/month. The conversion trigger is workflow automation — when teams see the value of auto-created Jira tickets, they upgrade for unlimited meetings and custom routing rules.

name: Driftwood
tagline: Project management for teams that think in documents, not tickets
description: Driftwood is a document-first project management tool where specs, tasks, and status updates live in the same rich-text workspace. It's what happens when Notion and Linear have a baby that actually ships on time.
mission:
There are two types of project management tools in the world: ticket trackers and document platforms. Jira and Linear are great at tracking work items but terrible at capturing the context behind them. Notion and Coda are great at documentation but their project management features feel bolted on.

Driftwood merges these worlds. We believe that a task without context is just busywork, and a document without accountability is just a wiki page. Every Driftwood project starts with a spec — a rich document that captures the what, why, and how. Tasks are extracted from the spec and tracked inline. As the spec evolves, tasks stay in sync. As tasks are completed, the spec reflects progress.

Our founding team built product at companies where the gap between "the document" and "the board" caused real problems. Engineers worked off stale specs. PMs updated documents that nobody checked. Status meetings existed solely to bridge the gap between what was written and what was happening.

Driftwood eliminates that gap by making documents and tasks the same thing. Your spec is your project plan is your status dashboard. We're building for teams that think in prose and paragraphs, not just checkboxes and story points.
marketResearch:
The project management software market is $7.2B, growing at 13% CAGR. The knowledge management/collaborative docs market adds $3.4B. The intersection — document-centric project management — is an emerging category with an estimated TAM of $2.8B. Our SAM targets 10-200 person teams at product-led companies that use both Notion (or Confluence) and Linear (or Jira), representing $800M. Initial SOM targeting early-stage startups and SMBs is $130M.

Competitors: Linear (excellent task tracking, minimal document capabilities), Notion (strong docs, weak project tracking), Asana (feature-rich but complex), Height (AI-powered but still ticket-first). Driftwood differentiates by making the document the atomic unit of project management — tasks emerge from documents rather than existing in a separate system.

Target user: product managers, engineering leads, and founders at 10-200 person companies who currently maintain both a documentation tool and a project tracker. Our insight is that they'd prefer one tool that does both well rather than two tools that need constant syncing.

GTM: PLG with a generous free tier (up to 5 users). Teams adopt for a single project, realize the document-task integration saves them from maintaining two tools, and expand to team-wide adoption. Pricing is per-workspace-member, competitive with Linear + Notion combined pricing.

name: Arcline
description: Arcline lets development teams branch their database the way they branch code. Create isolated database copies for every feature branch, run migrations safely, and merge schema changes without stepping on each other.
mission:
Git solved collaboration for code. But databases are still a shared mutable resource that everyone tiptoes around. Every developer on the team either shares a staging database (and breaks each other's work) or maintains a local database (and falls out of sync). Migrations are tested by crossing fingers. Schema conflicts are discovered at merge time.

Arcline brings the branching paradigm to databases. When you create a feature branch, Arcline creates a corresponding database branch — an isolated, full-fidelity copy of your database that you can migrate, seed, and test against without affecting anyone else. When your code merges, your database changes merge too, with conflict detection and resolution built in.

We're not building another database hosting platform. We're building a workflow layer that sits between your application and your database, making the development experience match what engineers already expect from their code workflow. Branch, develop, test, merge — for data, not just code.

Our team built developer tools at PlanetScale and Neon and saw firsthand that database branching isn't just a nice-to-have — it's the missing piece of the modern development workflow. We started Arcline because we believe databases should be as easy to collaborate on as code.
marketResearch:
The database-as-a-service market is $18B and growing at 20% CAGR. Within this, developer workflow tools for databases — migration management, branching, schema design — represent an emerging $1.5B segment. Our TAM spans all development teams using relational databases, roughly $1.5B. Our SAM focuses on teams of 10-200 developers using PostgreSQL or MySQL in cloud environments, approximately $500M. Initial SOM targeting mid-market tech companies is $80M.

Competitors: PlanetScale (branching for MySQL, shutting down free tier, Vitess complexity), Neon (PostgreSQL branching but focused on serverless compute, not workflow), Atlas (Terraform for databases, migration-focused), Prisma (ORM with migrate tool, no branching). Arcline differentiates by supporting multiple database engines (Postgres, MySQL, SQLite) and focusing on the complete branch-develop-merge workflow rather than just infrastructure.

Target users: backend engineers and platform teams at companies running relational databases. Our wedge is migration safety — teams adopt Arcline to test migrations on branched databases before running them in production. The expansion motion is full branching adoption for development workflows.

GTM: open-core model. The CLI and local branching are free and open-source. Cloud sync, team collaboration, and CI/CD integration are paid features. Pricing is per-developer-seat plus storage.

faqs.question: How fast is branch creation?
faqs.answer: Sub-second for databases up to 50GB using copy-on-write snapshots. You only pay storage for the rows that differ between branches.

faqs.question: Does it work with my existing ORM?
faqs.answer: Yes — Arcline works at the connection level. Your ORM (Prisma, Drizzle, SQLAlchemy, etc.) connects to the branch database as if it were any other database.

faqs.question: What about production?
faqs.answer: Arcline is for development and CI environments. We don't touch production. But you can use branch databases to safely test production migration scripts before running them.

faqs.answer: The CLI and local branching engine are fully open-source (Apache 2.0). Cloud sync, team features, and CI/CD integration are paid.

name: Haystack
tagline: Internal search that actually finds things
description: Haystack is a unified search engine for your company's internal tools. Search across Notion, Slack, Google Drive, Jira, Confluence, and GitHub from a single bar. Find the thing, not ten tabs.
mission:
The average knowledge worker uses 13 different SaaS tools. Each tool has its own search — and each search only sees what's inside that tool. When you're looking for "that doc Sarah shared about the Q3 pricing strategy," you have to guess whether it's in Notion, Google Docs, Slack, or email. You open four tabs and search four times.

Haystack replaces those four searches with one. We index your company's internal tools — Notion, Slack, Google Drive, Jira, Confluence, GitHub, Linear, and more — into a unified search layer that understands context, permissions, and relevance. One search bar. One answer.

But search is just the beginning. Once we've indexed your company's knowledge, we can do things that individual tool search can't: find information that spans multiple tools, surface knowledge that's about to become stale, and answer questions using your company's collective intelligence.

We started Haystack because we lived in the world of tab-switching and context-guessing that every knowledge worker experiences. We believe that internal search should be as good as Google — but for your company's private knowledge.
marketResearch:
The enterprise search market is valued at $5.2B in 2025, growing at 14% CAGR. The subset focused on SaaS-native unified search — tools that connect to cloud applications rather than on-premise systems — is a $1.8B opportunity growing at 22% CAGR. Our TAM is the broader enterprise search market. Our SAM targets companies with 50-5,000 employees using 5+ SaaS tools, approximately $900M. Initial SOM is $140M focusing on tech companies and knowledge-work organizations.

Competitors: Glean (raised $260M, dominant in enterprise AI search but priced for large enterprises at $10+ per user/month), Dashworks (smaller competitor, good UX but limited connector coverage), Guru (knowledge management focused, less search-oriented), and native search within platforms (limited to single-tool scope). Haystack differentiates through three vectors: aggressive pricing ($4/user/month vs Glean's $10+), faster onboarding (most connectors activate in under 2 minutes), and a developer API that lets teams build internal search into their own tools.

Target buyer: IT admins and operations leaders who field "where do I find X?" questions daily. Our PLG motion starts with individuals connecting personal instances of tools (free for up to 3 connectors), converting to team plans when admins connect organization-wide accounts with permission syncing.

name: Litmus
tagline: Visual regression testing that doesn't cry wolf
description: Litmus catches UI bugs before users do. It takes intelligent screenshots of your app across browsers and screen sizes, diffs them against your baseline, and only alerts on visual changes that actually matter — ignoring dynamic content, animations, and rendering noise.
mission:
Visual regression testing has a reputation problem. Teams try it, get buried in false positives — a timestamp changed, a loading spinner was mid-rotation, an ad shifted by 2 pixels — and turn it off. The idea is right but the execution has been terrible.

Litmus fixes visual testing by being smart about what constitutes a real change. Our diffing engine uses perceptual comparison models trained on real UI components to distinguish meaningful visual regressions from harmless rendering variance. A button that moved from the left to the center of a card? That's a regression. A tooltip that rendered 1ms later? That's noise.

We're a team of frontend engineers and QA specialists who got tired of either maintaining flaky visual tests or shipping UI bugs to production. We built Litmus because we believe visual testing should be like a senior QA engineer: observant enough to catch real issues, experienced enough to ignore noise.

Our goal is to make visual testing a reliable, always-on part of every CI pipeline. Not something teams try and abandon, but something they trust as deeply as their unit tests.
marketResearch:
The testing tools market is valued at $8.3B in 2025 with visual testing tools representing approximately $600M of that, growing at 30% CAGR as frontend complexity increases. Our TAM is the broader visual testing market. Our SAM targets web application teams with CI/CD pipelines running automated tests, approximately $350M. Initial SOM focusing on React/Next.js teams is $60M.

Competitors: Percy (Browserstack-owned, market leader but plagued by false positives), Chromatic (Storybook-focused, great for component libraries but limited for full-page testing), Applitools (enterprise pricing, AI-based but expensive at $60+/user/month), and Playwright's built-in screenshot comparison (free but requires heavy manual configuration). Litmus differentiates through perceptual AI that reduces false positives by 85% compared to pixel-based diffing, sub-10-minute feedback in CI, and pricing accessible to small teams ($19/month flat for up to 5,000 snapshots).

Target users: frontend engineers and QA leads at companies with 5-50 developers. Our wedge is the team that tried Percy, got burned by false positives, and turned off visual testing. Litmus gives them a second chance with testing that actually works.

GTM: developer-led. Free tier supports 500 snapshots/month. Integration with GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket PRs. Screenshots appear inline as PR checks, making adoption frictionless.

name: Conduit
tagline: Real-time data pipelines you can set up in an afternoon
description: Conduit is a managed data streaming platform that connects databases, APIs, and SaaS tools into real-time pipelines. Change data capture, transformations, and delivery — without managing Kafka or writing Flink jobs.
mission:
Every company is a data company now. But moving data between systems in real-time still requires a PhD in distributed systems or a six-figure Confluent contract. Teams that need their Postgres changes reflected in Elasticsearch within seconds — not hours — are stuck choosing between managed Kafka (expensive, complex) or batch ETL (slow, stale).

Conduit makes real-time data movement as simple as connecting two endpoints and defining a transformation. We handle the hard parts — change data capture, exactly-once delivery, schema evolution, backpressure, and failure recovery — so your team can focus on what the data does, not how it moves.

We're engineers who spent years building and maintaining data infrastructure at companies where Kafka was simultaneously the most critical and most feared system in the stack. We saw teams avoid real-time architectures because the operational overhead was too high, even when their products desperately needed fresh data.

Conduit's mission is to democratize real-time data. Not just for companies that can afford a dedicated data platform team, but for any team that needs data in the right place at the right time.
marketResearch:
The data integration and ETL market is valued at $14.2B, with real-time streaming and CDC representing the fastest-growing segment at 28% CAGR. Our TAM includes all companies needing real-time data movement between systems, approximately $6B. Our SAM focuses on mid-market companies (100-5,000 employees) that need real-time pipelines but can't justify dedicated data platform teams, roughly $2B. Initial SOM targeting tech companies replacing batch ETL with streaming is $300M.

Competitors: Confluent/Kafka (the default for streaming, but complex and expensive for mid-market), Fivetran (dominant in batch ETL, adding streaming but it's not their strength), Airbyte (open-source ETL, good community but limited real-time capabilities), Estuary (CDC-focused, closest to our positioning). Conduit differentiates through radical simplicity — a web UI where you connect source to destination, define transforms in SQL, and deploy in minutes — combined with production-grade reliability underneath.

Target buyer: data engineers and backend engineers who need real-time data movement but don't want to operate Kafka. Our PLG motion offers a free tier with up to 1M events/month. Teams upgrade when they need higher throughput, more connectors, and SLAs.
